title: How to build an AI-Native Health Company — Dan Feng, Maven Clinic
talk_summary: Dan Feng describes Maven Clinic's two-year transition to an AI-native company: enabling AI tools for the middle-majority of staff, changing hiring/reward and sprint-based planning, and shifting engineers from writing to reviewing/architecting code. The most concrete engineering lessons are risk-tiered AI adoption, PR-size and self-merge review policy, and reliability practices like multi-model agreement and repeated integration-test pass rates for LLM features.

takeaways.technique: Risk-tiered PR review with self-merge and size caps
takeaways.what_they_do: Engineers self-identify whether a PR needs human review; simple confident PRs merge without review but the author stays accountable. Reviewed PRs are capped at ~500 lines and large features are stacked into multiple PRs, explicitly to avoid rubber-stamp approvals.
takeaways.evidence_quote: each PR shouldn't have more than 500 lines of code because nobody can do a meaningful code review

takeaways.technique: Repeated-run pass-rate thresholds for LLM tests
takeaways.what_they_do: Because LLM behavior is nondeterministic, each integration test is run many times and must sustain a high pass rate rather than passing once. They maintain hundreds of integration tests covering known use cases and keep adding to the suite.
takeaways.evidence_quote: not only pass once is not good enough anymore, because the LLM can do different things... we consistently requires a high pass rate, like for example, 90%
takeaways.numbers: ~90% pass rate across repeated runs; hundreds of integration tests

takeaways.what_they_do: For irreversible/high-cost actions (e.g., reimbursement amounts) they run the same input through different models and only proceed when results agree; on disagreement they escalate to a human rather than guess.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we will use different models to review the same receipt. We only move forward if the results from different models agree

takeaways.technique: Risk classification of acceptable vs unacceptable failures
takeaways.what_they_do: Before building, they classify which AI failures are tolerable (user can retry) versus intolerable (financial/irreversible), and only add heavy safeguards (multi-model checks, human handoff) to the latter.
takeaways.evidence_quote: identify which failures is acceptable, which ones are not acceptable

takeaways.technique: Short sprint horizons with 1-2 page specs
takeaways.what_they_do: They stopped long PRD/TDD cycles and multi-month planning; PMs specify only the next 2-4 week sprint in 1-2 pages, engineers ship within the sprint, and it's acceptable to reverse a two-week-old decision. Long-term plans are directional inspiration only.

takeaways.technique: Risk-ascending adoption of AI coding tools
takeaways.what_they_do: They introduced AI coding first on lowest-risk, easily verifiable tasks (unit tests, docs) to build confidence and codify rules/skills, then expanded to all engineering tasks, and investigate when engineers opt out.
takeaways.evidence_quote: We started with the lowest risk task, like starting with writing unit tests, documentation
